source_text: Instruxit acerrime disputationem magister egregius, et spem nobis de consortio Mediatoris ingessit, asserens illum hominem, quantum spectat ad substantiam qua nobis iungitur, nihil exceptum habuisse, opinionemque quam infidelitas sciscebat, non minus Christo praeiudicare posse quam nobis. Sic ergo miscet negotium Christi et hominum, ut necesse sit in utraque parte credi, quod in altera censeatur. Opinati quippe fuerant per idem tempus homines, quia resurrectio mortuorum futura non esset; non tamen resurrexisse Christum negabant. Arripit hoc Magister Gentium, et pronuntiat necesse esse ut uni praeiudicio pars utraque sit pervia, et aut omnes homines resurrecturi, aut nec Christus resurrexisse credatur. Certe hanc vim in disputando Apostolus non haberet, si secundum Manichaeos et eorum discipulos Traducianos, carnem Christi a naturae nostrae communione distingueret.
pass_a_gloss: The outstanding teacher instructed the disputation most sharply, and poured into us a hope from the fellowship of the Mediator, asserting that that human, as far as it looks to the substance by which he is joined to us, had nothing excepted, and that the opinion which infidelity was inquiring could prejudge not less Christ than us. Thus therefore he mixes the business of Christ and of humans, so that it is necessary that what is judged in one part be believed in each. For humans at the same time had opined that a resurrection of the dead would not be future; they nevertheless were not denying that Christ had risen. The Teacher of the Nations snatches this, and pronounces it necessary that each part be passable to one prior judgment, and either all humans about to rise, or not even Christ believed to have risen. Certainly the Apostle would not have this force in disputing, if according to the Manichaeans and their disciples the Traducians he distinguished Christ's flesh from the communion of our nature.

lemmas.lexica: Julian's polemic label for teachers of tradux peccati
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: The outstanding teacher built his argument with great force and gave us hope through our shared condition with the Mediator. He maintained that this man, as regards the substance by which he is joined to us, possessed no exemption, and that the opinion adopted by unbelief could prejudice Christ no less than us. He therefore joins Christ’s case and humanity’s so closely that what is judged in one must necessarily be believed in the other.

At that time people had thought there would be no resurrection of the dead, yet they did not deny that Christ had risen. The Teacher of the Gentiles seizes this and pronounces that both sides must be open to the same judgment: either all humans are to rise, or Christ must be believed not to have risen. The apostle certainly would not have this argumentative force if, according to the Manichaeans and their disciples who teach inherited sin, he separated Christ’s flesh from participation in our nature (1 Corinthians 15:12–17).

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
